A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and retain identifiable theory and experiments. Their text, equations, figures, and complete appendices A–C are readable and support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original TinyStories masked-language-model training and numerical experiments on attention, token similarity, and initialization, including supplementary experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains original training and simulation results and adds gradient measurements and a vanilla-versus-gain-controlled attention training comparison.

M1.justification: v2 adds gain-controlled attention, which subtracts the sequence mean of the values from the attention output, and extends the propagation procedure to pre-norm architectures (Section 5; Algorithms 2–3). Algorithm 1 largely repackages the existing post-norm recurrence, but the additional architectural procedures are substantive.

E1.justification: Both versions use TinyStories masked language modeling and numerical attention/signal-propagation experiments. The added architectural and gradient experiments retain this coverage; changing sequence lengths, widths, and normalization placement does not introduce another dataset or task.

E2.justification: v2 adds a direct vanilla post-LN comparator for gain-controlled post-LN training in Figure C.1. Figure 4 also compares theoretical predictions for vanilla and gain-controlled pre-/post-LN variants. These are limited architectural comparisons; cited shaped-transformer methods are not independently benchmarked.

E3.justification: v2 introduces gradient-norm scaling tests across sequence lengths 2048, 4096, and 8192 and dimensions 256, 512, and 1024. Its new attention comparison specifies a single-head, dimension-480 model trained for 0.5 epochs. Existing experimental settings are retained, although the new comparison's depth is inconsistently described as 20 versus 30 layers.

E4.justification: v2 adds gradient-scaling sensitivity analysis, normalization-placement and value-centering comparisons, and training validation of gain-controlled attention. It removes v1 Appendix C.3's no-residual propagation study. The lower-learning-rate analysis remains, and the tanh analysis moves from the main text to Appendix C.4.

E5.justification: Figure 1 retains averages over 10 random initializations and 10 input sequences with standard-deviation error bars. The relocated tanh experiment retains 25 initializations and 10 sequences per initialization. The new figures introduce no specified seed counts, repeated-run information, or uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds gradient curves showing small-beta suppression and scaling collapse, normalization/centering predictions, and Figure C.1's new comparison showing final loss approximately 1 for gain-controlled attention versus 6 for vanilla attention. The original principal plots, including the relocated tanh results, retain their results; the no-residual study's results are removed.

T1.justification: v2 adds query/key-gradient Result 2 and its Appendix B.4 derivation, extends the forward analysis to a norm-dependent critical threshold, and develops pre-norm and centered-attention recursions. It also introduces the distinction between CLT breakdown at beta_c/2 and the transition at beta_c. The new gradient derivation uses a bound and an additional scaling assumption despite the main text's exact-expression claim.

C1.justification: The unified rank/entropy-collapse explanation and initialization guidance remain. v2 additionally claims an exact backward-gradient characterization, applicability across normalization placements, and evidence that gain-controlled attention avoids both failure modes, substantially broadening the contributions beyond v1's focus on vanilla forward propagation.

C2.justification: Section 3.3 newly explains how residual-path gradients change initially independent embeddings and enable learning despite suppressed query/key gradients. v2 interprets normalization placement and value centering as remedies, qualifies gain-controlled training evidence as preliminary, and newly warns that the tanh chaotic regime entails exploding gradients and unstable training.

D1.justification: v2 supplies explicit block-update pseudocode and training specifications for the gain-controlled comparison, while removing v1 Appendix B.1's effective-temperature conversion and BERT example. Existing hardware, runtime, and optimizer disclosures are largely unchanged. The new experiment's conflicting 20-/30-layer descriptions limit reproducibility.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly credits Lucibello and Mézard with the attention–REM mapping and locates its novelty in applying that mapping to signal propagation. It expands positioning around the complementary infinite-sequence limit and discusses gain control relative to Naderi et al. Several earlier references, including Dinan et al., are removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, setup, and retained theoretical exposition are substantially rewritten. v1's three-step derivation becomes named forward/backward results followed by separate full-block analysis, applications, and conclusions; the appendices are reorganized around results and algorithms.

P2.justification: v2 removes the architecture schematic and v1 Figures B.2 and C.3, expands the entropy/training figure with a gradient panel, and adds normalization and gain-control figures plus three pseudocode displays. The tanh figure moves to the appendix, and retained figures are resized and rearranged.

improvement.justification: The new algorithms, gradient analysis, and attention comparison add useful scope and practical evidence. However, Result 2 is claimed as exact while Appendix B.4 provides a bound followed by an assumed scaling; the new appendix cosine-update formula also disagrees with Eq. (11). Together with the conflicting 20-/30-layer descriptions of the gain-control experiment, these issues undermine confidence in important additions. The benefits and unresolved theoretical and reporting problems prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
